SKYWALKER 3046 IS A SPACECRAFT

DESIGNED TO COLLECT DEBRİS FROM

BROKEN SATELLITES IN SPACE AND

BRING IT BACK TO EARTH. EQUİPPED

WİTH AN ONBOARD TELESCOPE, IT WİLL

ALSO ASSIST IN THE DISCOVERY OF

EXOPLANETS, AND IT WLL OPERATE

USİNG A HYBRİD SYSTEM OF SOLAR

ENERGY AND CONVENTİONAL FUEL.

3

WHERE IS THE FUEL

REFILLED?

IT CAN BE REFILLED IN THE

SPECIAL FUEL SECTION

LOCATED ON THE

INTERNATIONAL SPACE STATION.

4

HOW IT WORKS ?

IT RETRIEVES SATELLITE

COMPONENTS FROM A

SPECIAL COMPARTMENT ON

ITS UNDERSIDE, RECHARGES

ITSELF USING SOLAR PANELS,

AND—IN ITS AIRPLANE

CONFIGURATION—CAN

EXPLORE THE PLANETS OF THE

SOLAR SYSTEM.

5

If the "Skywalker 3046" becomes a reality, we could explore the planets in our solar system more closely. Furthermore, it could collect

debris from satellites for recycling, and signals could be transmitted more rapidly to spacecraft like Voyager.

EFFECTS

Here is the translation of the notable NASA satellites and space telescopes that failed, retired, or deorbited between 2000 and 2026:

1. Earth Observation and Climate Satellites

UARS (Upper Atmosphere Research Satellite - September 2011): This massive 6-ton research satellite was launched to study the upper

atmosphere. Years after its mission ended, it made an uncontrolled reentry into Earth's atmosphere, falling into the Pacific Ocean.

ICESat (Ice, Cloud and land Elevation Satellite - February 2010): Designed to measure polar ice sheets and sea levels, this NASA satellite

experienced laser system failures and was safely deorbited to burn up in the atmosphere after completing its mission.

2. Solar and Space Telescopes

Kepler Space Telescope (November 2018): Famous for discovering thousands of exoplanets (planets outside our solar system), this legendary

telescope ran out of fuel and lost its pointing control, prompting NASA to retire it in deep space.

Spitzer Space Telescope (January 2020): Observing the universe in infrared wavelengths, this telescope exhausted its liquid coolant and could

no longer transmit useful science data, leading NASA to permanently shut it down.

RHESSI Satellite (April 2023): Launched in 2002 to study solar flares and high-energy X-rays, this satellite spent roughly 21 years in space

before making an uncontrolled reentry and burning up in the atmosphere.

3. Cosmology and Deep Space Crafts

COBE (Cosmic Background Explorer - January 2008): A groundbreaking NASA satellite that studied the remnants of the Big Bang (cosmic

microwave background radiation); after years of passive inactivity, it was completely decommissioned.

TIMED Satellite (January 2024): Studying the upper layers of Earth's atmosphere, this satellite made headlines due to communication glitches

and a close-call collision risk with a defunct Russian satellite, though it continues to operate.

Total Count (2000–2026): Out of the 7 NASA missions listed above, 6 are completely defunct, retired, or deorbited (UARS, ICESat, Kepler, Spitzer,

RHESSI, and COBE), while 1 (TIMED) remains operational despite experiencing technical glitches and orbital hazards. (Note: Globally, hundreds of

smaller NASA CubeSats and commercial satellites have also failed or burned up during this 26-year span).
